scope: Read-only review of official MCP, Microsoft Playwright MCP, Chromium, and Blender sources mapped to the current Windows endpoint kit and task-local desktop tests. No endpoint policy, OS setting, firewall rule, browser profile, application preference, or certificate was changed. No additional negative security test was run.

catalog_dedup.search: Searched research/llm-wiki/catalogs, papers, sources, analysis/local-tools, and desktop experiments for T01/T02/T21, MCP auth, annotations, Playwright allowed origins/file access/unsafe tools, Chromium sandbox, Blender scripting security.

references.title: MCP Authorization 2026-07-28; Tools 2026-07-28; Security Best Practices 2026-07-28
references.license: Protocol/specification reference; no executable package license asserted
read_scope: Authorization: Purpose and Scope; Protocol Requirements; Scope Selection Strategy; canonical resource URI; bearer token requirements and audience/scope validation; HTTP 401/403 and insufficient-scope guidance.
Tools: User Interaction Model; tool definition annotations; statement that clients MUST treat tool annotations as untrusted unless from trusted servers; Security Considerations.

Security Best Practices: Local MCP Server Compromise; risks of arbitrary code under MCP-client privileges; recommends least-privilege sandboxing; says stdio limits access to MCP client and HTTP should use auth tokens or restricted IPC.
official_claim: Authorization is optional. If an MCP implementation uses HTTP, it SHOULD follow the authorization specification; stdio implementations SHOULD NOT follow that HTTP OAuth flow and should instead obtain credentials from the environment.

For HTTP OAuth, the client sends a bearer token on each request; the MCP resource server validates that the token is intended for its resource/audience and enforces scope. A loopback address alone is not a bearer identity or per-tool permission model.
Tool annotations are descriptive metadata; clients MUST consider them untrusted unless the server is trusted. The tools page recommends user confirmation for sensitive tool operations.

The local-server security guide warns that a local server may access the user system and may be accessible to other local processes; it describes execution with the MCP client’s privileges and recommends sandboxing, least privilege, stdio or authenticated/restricted local IPC.
references.application: For this kit, record transport and OS identity separately: `endpoint-agent/agent.py::describe` marks local configured command servers as stdio and hashes their command, while HTTP endpoints are represented by a redacted endpoint reference; `probe_mcp` sends only one initialize request to an HTTP candidate. These are inventory/probe functions, not a process sandbox or a per-tool authorization layer. Classify actual effects from the pinned server source and observed socket/process/filesystem reach, never from `readOnlyHint` or tool text alone. The Windows named-pipe broker has a per-enrolled-account DACL for header forwarding, but it is distinct from restricting an MCP server’s own process capabilities.
limitations: The fixed protocol text defines requirements and recommendations but does not prove that a particular MCP client/server implements them.
The JSON-RPC stdio transport narrows which client speaks the protocol; it does not restrict the child process’s file, network, registry, or process privileges.
An OAuth resource/audience/scope check applies only where the HTTP MCP server implements it. It does not automatically mediate a desktop plugin’s separate raw loopback bridge.

code_targets.observation: Transport classification distinguishes configured HTTP from local stdio but does not show effective process containment or token/tool scope.
HTTP detector deliberately sends one initialize request; it is not a tools/list or tools/call authorization check.
Named pipe DACL limits credential-header broker access to the enrolled account plus SYSTEM/owner; this is not the child MCP server sandbox.

references.title: Microsoft Playwright MCP README and tool documentation
read_scope: Pinned README lines 410-411: --allowed-origins is not a security boundary and does not constrain redirects; unrestricted file-access switch and default workspace-root/CWD restriction; file:// navigation default blocked.
Pinned README line 435 and session documentation around lines 464-489: isolated in-memory profile option and profile/session behavior.
Pinned README lines 1074-1080: browser_run_code_unsafe executes arbitrary JS in the Playwright MCP server process and is RCE-equivalent.
Pinned README tool table: browser navigation and UI actions; filesystem upload/drop; page JavaScript and network request metadata tools.
official_claim: --allowed-origins is a browser-request filter, not a security boundary; redirects are not constrained by it.

By default, local file access is limited to workspace roots (or current working directory if no roots are configured), and file:// navigation is blocked; --allow-unrestricted-file-access removes that restriction.
--isolated keeps browser profile state in memory; it describes profile persistence, not a separate Windows identity or OS sandbox.
browser_run_code_unsafe executes arbitrary code in the MCP server process; page evaluation and upload/drop also create distinct page and host-file access surfaces.
references.application: The validated Playwright runner uses stdio, headless Chromium, a task-local profile, and an exact random loopback origin in `run-playwright-mcp.mjs`. That verifies local fixture navigation/read only. It does not test redirects, arbitrary file access, browser_run_code_unsafe, or OS sandboxing. Keep unrestricted-file-access absent; deny file tools and unsafe-code tool at the client policy boundary unless explicitly needed; add a redirect-to-second-origin negative test to verify whether policy lives in the client/MCP route rather than assuming the origin option enforces it.
limitations: The README documents intended CLI behavior but does not prove the current client’s tool allow/deny policy or Chromium’s runtime sandbox state.
Origin filters do not restrict direct API/network calls made by page code or the MCP process, and the documentation explicitly excludes redirect enforcement.
Headless mode and an in-memory profile are not an operating-system account, network, or filesystem sandbox.

code_targets.observation: Runner binds its fixture to loopback and allows only its exact origin; this is test scope, not a policy boundary for all targets.
Tool effect inventory records execute/read/write/network capability per actual advertised schema.

references.title: Chromium: Unsandboxed Processes by Platform
references.version: Chromium source commit f68f02e31715f9fd8b54fc45d46f94e1e56d2985; document states table last updated for M128
read_scope: Lines 1-8 scope and statement that table tracks default Stable channel and is last updated for M128; lines 20-27 Browser/Network sandbox status; lines 41-44 renderer sandbox status.
official_claim: The cited table marks the Browser process unsandboxed on all platforms and the Network process unsandboxed on Windows; it marks renderer, extensions, and PDF renderer processes sandboxed.
The source states that its process table was last updated for milestone 128; it is a process-boundary reference, not proof of sandbox status for the bundled Chromium 155.0.8059.12 runtime.
references.application: Do not treat a sandboxed Chromium renderer as containment for the Playwright MCP Node server, Burp extension, Blender MCP process, or browser process. The task uses Windows; independently inspect runtime process flags/token/job/AppContainer state before claiming a Chromium OS boundary. The endpoint kit’s per-account egress firewall can reduce outbound network access, but its README explicitly notes loopback is not filtered and its Windows kit does not install App Control/AppLocker policies.
limitations: The document’s process table is dated M128 despite a later source commit; the actual tested browser is Chromium 155.0.8059.12, so current runtime process sandbox state remains unverified.
This source describes Chromium child-process sandbox categories, not a guarantee about every browser process, Playwright MCP process, profile option, plugin, or desktop bridge.
No token, AppContainer, job-object, or browser command-line sandbox inspection was run in this read-only review.

code_targets.observation: Account-scoped egress/firewall and named-pipe controls are documented; loopback is not blocked and App Control/AppLocker is not installed.
Process inventory detects local stdio servers; detection is not containment.
Node MCP child process shares launcher identity unless an OS boundary is separately configured.

references.title: Blender 5.2 LTS Manual: Scripting & Security
references.version: Blender manual version 5.2 LTS; Blender application actually tested at 5.2.2 LTS
read_scope: HTML section Scripting & Security and its Auto Execution / Manual Execution headings; `-Y` and `--disable-autoexec` option text.
official_claim: Blender Python does not restrict what a script can do; only scripts from known and trusted sources should be run.
Automatic execution of scripts in blend files is disabled by default; registered text blocks and animation drivers are described as auto-execution paths.
Auto-run can be disabled by `-Y` or `--disable-autoexec`, but interactive/manual scripting such as the text editor remains an execution path.
references.application: The tested Blender add-on bridge is a raw TCP listener observed at 127.0.0.1:9876 without authentication or Origin checks; its `execute_code` path reaches unrestricted Python `exec`. Blender’s autoexec default protects against auto-running embedded .blend scripts; it does not constrain explicit MCP/bridge Python execution. The current task-local launcher uses `--factory-startup` but omits `--disable-autoexec`; add that switch for any future validation that opens untrusted .blend files, while retaining the understanding that the MCP code tool remains arbitrary code execution with the process token’s permissions.
limitations: The manual is guidance, not proof of the installed preference or process command-line flags; this report did not inspect or alter global Blender preferences.
The manual’s auto-execution control does not sandbox explicitly invoked add-on or MCP Python.
The observed loopback bridge had no per-caller authentication; loopback limits remote routability, not access by other local processes.

code_targets.observation: Portable Blender launches hidden with factory startup and the task profile; future untrusted-file runs should add `--disable-autoexec`.
Actual accepted call executed arbitrary Python to add a synthetic sphere and changed the scene from one mesh to two.
Observed address, missing auth/Origin checks, safe-mode route limit, and unrestricted socket command are recorded separately.

findings.finding: HTTP OAuth scope/audience, stdio environment credentials, tool annotations, and the local process OS identity are separate control planes. `readOnlyHint`, command hashing, a successful initialize response, or stdio itself does not prove least-privilege behavior.
findings.application: Keep the endpoint kit’s transport inventory and initialize-only detection as inventory evidence. Authorization decisions must bind HTTP token audience/scope at the gateway route; local tool effects must be derived from the actual source and caller identity. The named-pipe DACL is only for the header broker, not an OS sandbox for the harness or MCP child.

validation_criteria.criterion: An allowed HTTP request with the endpoint-specific audience and minimum scope succeeds through the managed gateway route; record token claims only in redacted test evidence.
Wrong-audience, missing-token, and insufficient-scope requests fail with the expected 401/403 boundary; a tool declaring readOnlyHint does not bypass server-side denial of a prohibited effect.
A local stdio child launched under the same account cannot be described as isolated absent separate OS evidence; test file/network/process denial under a distinct restricted identity or OS sandbox.

findings.finding: The exact Playwright MCP build offers a non-boundary origin filter, host file tools, and a tool that executes arbitrary JavaScript in the server process. Isolated profile mode is profile-state management, not OS containment.
findings.application: Keep the tested loopback-only synthetic fixture claim narrow; enforce tool allowlists, no unrestricted file flag, and URL/network policy outside the Playwright origin filter. A different local or remote MCP target must not be inferred to be denied because the allowed-origin parameter was set.

validation_criteria.criterion: Headless `browser_navigate` + `browser_snapshot` read the generated loopback fixture via stdio and task-local profile.
Have the fixture redirect to a second synthetic loopback origin; prove the enforcement layer, if any, blocks the redirect. Exercise no user or public target.

Under a temporary restricted identity, verify denied reads/writes to a canary path outside the allowed workspace and denied egress beyond a local fixture; test that unsafe-code and upload/drop calls are unavailable at client policy.

findings.finding: Blender auto-run protection is specifically about implicit scripts embedded in files; the MCP add-on’s explicit `execute_code` bridge executes Python and is an independent arbitrary-code surface. The observed loopback bind has no caller authentication/Origin check.
findings.application: Treat the bridge as code execution under the Blender process token. Use only a separate task profile and synthetic scene, retain optional external integrations disabled, and apply an OS/process boundary if this bridge is exposed to an agent. `--disable-autoexec` should be included before opening untrusted project files, but it does not restrict explicit MCP Python.

validation_criteria.criterion: Actual stdio MCP read calls succeeded; synthetic sphere write changed scene mesh count 1 to 2 and follow-up read located it.
Open only a synthetic file with a harmless registered startup marker under `--disable-autoexec`; confirm the marker does not execute, then do not infer restrictions on explicit MCP Python.

validation_criteria.status: partly observed: loopback listener and unauthenticated exec path; no second principal probe
validation_criteria.criterion: From a separate same-account process, establish whether 127.0.0.1:9876 accepts direct requests; then verify OS firewall/App Control/identity controls independently, without using real data.

findings.finding: A Chromium renderer sandbox, headless run, in-memory profile, Windows account-level egress rule, or named-pipe ACL must not be described as an OS sandbox for the whole MCP stack. The Chromium source reference explicitly marks browser/Windows network processes unsandboxed and renderer sandboxed, but its table is M128 and therefore not runtime proof for Chromium 155.
findings.application: For this kit, state which process token, network, filesystem, and local IPC boundary was observed. The Windows README says endpoint firewall rules do not block loopback and the kit does not install App Control/AppLocker; `stdio_processes` observes but does not contain stdio services. Plugin/raw bridge restrictions need their own bind/auth/Origin/DACL controls or a separately verified process sandbox.

validation_criteria.criterion: Inventory PID, executable path, user SID, parent, command flags, listener binds, and OS restriction state for the target server and app before asserting a boundary.
An unprivileged same-account process should be unable to invoke the bridge or read outside the fixture if that is the declared policy; if it can, report loopback or profile isolation as insufficient.
Run two controlled tests: one with client allowlist only and one with OS network/filesystem policy only, each using separate canary effects; retain results to distinguish policy-layer enforcement.

validation.performed: Source/catalog review and code-path mapping only; no security setting was changed, no negative test was run, and no claim of OS sandboxing was made.
